questions.q: What does the lesson recommend using a LinkedIn headline's roughly 220 characters for?
options: Searchable terms and a concrete claim, not just a repeated job title
A full paragraph describing your entire work history
Your phone number and home address
A list of every company you have ever applied to
questions.explain: The lesson specifically warns against wasting the headline on a repeated job title and recommends searchable terms plus a concrete claim.

questions.q: How does the lesson say a governance portfolio typically differs from a data-science-style GitHub portfolio?
options: It centers on documents and diagrams (glossary, RACI, lineage) rather than mostly runnable code
It should never include any SQL at all
It must be hosted exclusively on LinkedIn
It has no meaningful difference from a coding portfolio
questions.explain: The lesson explains that governance work mostly produces documents and diagrams, with a smaller amount of actual SQL, unlike a typical code-centric data science portfolio.

questions.q: Which Chapter 1 lessons does this lesson point to for the final strategy document and executive presentation deliverables?
options: Lessons 15 through 17
Lessons 1 through 3
Lesson 35
There are no such lessons in Chapter 1
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly references Chapter 1, Lessons 15 through 17 as walking through assembling and presenting those deliverables.

questions.q: According to the lesson, how should a candidate disclose that the capstone's organization (LTV Global) is fictional?
options: State it plainly, framing it as a strength that shows you can build a full governance program's scope
Avoid mentioning it and hope nobody asks
Claim the organization is real to seem more impressive
Only disclose it if directly and explicitly asked under oath
questions.explain: The lesson frames honest disclosure as protective and as a strength, not something to hide.

questions.q: Which of these is listed as a common mistake in this lesson?
options: A portfolio that is all policy prose with no concrete artifact, like actual glossary entries or SQL
Including a professional photo on LinkedIn
Writing an About section with more than one paragraph
Linking to a portfolio document from the Featured section
questions.explain: The lesson lists an all-prose, no-concrete-artifact portfolio as one of its named common mistakes.
